lines.text: Ask a chatbot the same question twice.
Same question. Same machine. A different answer. So which one did it actually mean?
Right now, hundreds of millions of people are asking machines things like this. Should I sign this? Is this rash normal? Is this email a scam?
And every answer, from ChatGPT to Claude, is built the same way: one word at a time. Each word, a small bet.
On September fifteenth, a startup called TypeSafe released an AI that refuses to play that game.
It's called Jev. It doesn't write a single word. It answers with a number.
Its makers claim it's up to a hundred times faster and cheaper than today's chatbots. And they raised forty million dollars on that bet.
So is this a better way for a machine to decide? To find out, we first have to look inside the ones we already use.
Take one question. An email arrives. Urgent! You have won a free cruise. Is it a scam?

You might think a chatbot knows its whole answer and simply types it out. It doesn't. Picture models like ChatGPT and Claude as little trains. They can't see their destination. They lay down their answer as track, one word at a time. Let's ride along with one.
At every junction, the track splits into possible next words. And each branch is exactly as wide as the chance of that word.
The train takes one. And only then can it see the next junction.
Each choice keeps only part of the width. So the chance of the whole sentence is whatever survives every junction. You multiply, one word at a time.
Quick test. Say every word is a safe bet, eighty percent likely. How likely is a whole sentence of twenty words? Take a guess.
About one percent. Twenty safe bets, multiplied together, leave almost nothing.
Mathematicians call this the chain rule. And it is, quite literally, how these models write.
The idea is older than any chatbot. In 1951, Claude Shannon, the father of information theory, gave people a passage of text and asked them to guess it, one letter at a time.
They were surprisingly good at it, because language is predictable. Every chatbot today plays Shannon's game, with words instead of letters, billions of times a day.
Usually, the train takes a wide branch. But every choice is a roll of the dice, and now and then, a thin one wins.
Totally. Four percent.
Four percent sounds like never. So how often does it actually happen? Let's run this junction a hundred times.
Four trains out of a hundred take the thin branch. Rare is not never. And across hundreds of millions of questions a day, rare happens all the time.
And every junction is shaped by the track already laid. After totally, the widest branch is... legit.
And just like that, the train has talked itself into a swamp. Fluent, confident, and wrong.
To be fair, real models usually get an email this obvious right. But the mechanism is real: every answer is a chain of small bets, and sometimes one goes bad.
Jev works differently. It never lays track, and it never says a word.
It takes in the whole letter in a single sweep, and splits all of its certainty between the only answers it is allowed to give.
Scam: zero point nine one. In one pass.
One of them writes. The other decides. Whether that's the future comes down to one question: can we trust that number? That's next time.
